Revision: keep loss=all fixed; test one memory-history mechanism next, not routing or updates.
Hypothesis: sparse top-k loop retrieval should preserve needed history while avoiding noisy full-history attention.
Discriminating control: full memory with identical loss/depth/width, differing only in top-k sparsity.
If topk does not beat full, the sparse-retrieval story is refuted for this tiny-model budget.

Frontier: prefix+loss=all is the only clear win; full/topk/retention/conf_bias/update_rank all fail to beat it.
Negative results: sparse top-k and low-rank updates are refuted as improvements; retention/full help revision but hurt repair.
Revision is the outlier: exact/ood improve with loop memory; pointer_chase, repair, proof_deps do not.
Two leading explanations: (A) uniform loop forcing is the active lever; (B) loop memory helps long-range state overwrite, not generic depth.
Separator: revision reordered keeps long-range overwrite pressure while removing clean event order.
Prediction: if (B) is right, full/retention memory should beat prefix on reordered revision; if (A) is right, it should not.
Keep length=28, depth=2, distract=6; total remains well under 96 tokens.
Control contrast: same spec with loss=all prefix memory vs full/retention memory.
A gain under reordering supports memory/state-tracking; a null gain supports loss/forcing as the cause.
Reordered revision is matched to ood_long but breaks clean-order advantage, so memory-specific gain is diagnostic.
